questions.q: A trader opens a large position on a perpetual swap protocol, then spends 30 minutes buying that asset on the thin external exchanges feeding the protocol's price oracle, pushing the oracle-reported price up 13x. The protocol then lets them borrow against the inflated paper value of their position. What's the root cause?
options: The protocol trusted an oracle price sourced from markets thin enough for the trader to move it directly, with no check on the size or speed of the move
The protocol's withdraw function sent funds before updating the trader's balance
The trader exploited a reentrancy bug in the lending contract
The protocol's smart contract had an unprotected selfdestruct function
questions.explain: Nothing was technically broken — every transaction executed as written. The vulnerability was trusting a price from markets the trader had enough capital to move himself.

questions.q: Why didn't the Mango Markets attacker need a flash loan, unlike the Harvest Finance attacker?
options: He used his own capital over a 30-minute window rather than needing to borrow and repay within a single atomic transaction
Flash loans don't exist on Solana
Mango Markets had a rule against flash loans
He partnered with Mango's own developers
questions.explain: The Harvest attack needed to borrow, manipulate, and undo everything within one transaction to repay the loan. Eisenberg's position didn't need to be reversed within a transaction, so he gradually moved the price with his own capital instead.

questions.q: What ultimately made Eisenberg's $110M+ extraction possible, mechanically?
options: The inflated oracle price made his long position's paper value enormous, and the protocol let him borrow against that inflated collateral
He found the private key to Mango's treasury wallet
He exploited an integer overflow in the swap contract's balance tracking
A Mango Markets employee approved the withdrawal manually
questions.explain: The protocol calculated his collateral value using the same oracle price he'd just manipulated, then let him borrow against that inflated number — draining the treasury of real assets in exchange for collateral that was never really worth what the oracle said.

questions.q: What's a practical mitigation this lesson describes for an asset with thin external liquidity?
options: A deviation check that compares the spot oracle price against a slower reference price (like a TWAP) and rejects values that moved too far, too fast
Increasing the protocol's gas limit
Requiring two-factor authentication before opening a position
Switching the protocol's programming language
questions.explain: A deviation check catches exactly this pattern — a price that moved far more, far faster, than legitimate trading would normally produce — without needing to predict the specific manipulation technique in advance.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the gap between "what the code technically allows" and "what the team intended" matters for review, using Eisenberg's own defense as the example?
options: Because he argued his trades were legal, protocol-compliant actions, which is exactly the kind of exploit that passes every require() check and still drains a protocol
Because he claimed a compiler bug caused the loss, which was later proven false
Because the protocol's legal terms of service were ambiguous about trading limits
Because he was a registered employee of Mango Markets at the time
questions.explain: A security review that only asks "does this code have bugs" misses this class of exploit entirely — every function executed correctly. The review also has to ask what a technically-valid sequence of actions is capable of doing, which is a design question, not just a correctness question.
